claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in high-entropy alloys increases lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion produces higher hardness.
Impeded dislocation motion produces higher yield strength.
Substitution with elements having different atomic radii can systematically vary atomic size mismatch.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can reflect local lattice distortion associated with atomic size mismatch.
Electron microscopy can measure or reveal local lattice distortion associated with atomic size mismatch.
Larger atomic size differences create stronger local strain fields.
Stronger local strain fields increase the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
The increased energy barrier results in enhanced dislocation pinning.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher hardness than a minimal-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with higher atomic size mismatch and greater lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than a minimal-mismatch baseline.
A minimal-atomic-size-mismatch baseline will have relatively low lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold when solid-solution strengthening dominates in single-phase high-entropy alloys under ambient conditions.
The proposed relationship may not hold when phase separation, precipitation, or other strengthening mechanisms dominate.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes substituting one or more elements while keeping the overall composition constant. Elemental substitution necessarily changes chemical identity, so only total atomic fraction or selected compositional ratios—not the full composition—can remain constant.
